<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm: intro endo}
    Denote by $\mathbb{K}(-),\mathbb{K}^{C_2}(-),\hat{\mathbb{K}}(-)$ the ungraded (classical), $C_2$-equivariant, and graded spectrum valued $K$-theory functors on the corresponding categories of (Real) $C^*$-algebras. Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra with a $C_2$-action $\alpha_A$. Then we have the following\footnote{the labels $\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2},\mathbf{3},\mathbf{4}$ are just notation and should not be confused with the multiplication with some constant maps!}.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There is a natural fiber sequence of spectra
        \[
        \mathbb{K}(A_u) \xrightarrow{\mathbf{1}} \mathbb{K}^{C_2}(A) \xrightarrow{\mathbf{2}} \hat{\mathbb{K}}(A)
        \tag{ABS}
        \]
         Here $(-)_u$ denotes the underlying $C^*$-algebra functor. Furthermore, the fiber sequence splits if $A$ is inner graded.
        \item There is a natural fiber sequence of spectra
        \[
        \hat{\mathbb{K}}(A) \xrightarrow{\mathbf{3}}\mathbb{K}^{C_2}(A) \xrightarrow{\mathbf{4}} \mathbb{K}((A \hat\otimes Cl^{0,2})_u) \tag{van Daele}
        \]
        Here $A \hat\otimes Cl^{0,2}$ denotes the graded tensor product of $A$ and $Cl^{0,2}$, the Clifford algebra on two generators which square to $+1$. If $A$ is inner graded, the fiber sequence splits.
        \item There are endomorphisms of the different $K$-theory spectra of $A$ arising from the above two fiber sequences. At the level of $\pi_0$, their effect can be concretely described when the algebra $A$ is unital:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $\mathbf{3} \circ \mathbf{2} \in \operatorname{End}(K_0^{C_2})(A)$ is given by mapping the class of a $C_2$-equivariant projective $A$-module $[M,\alpha_M] \in K_0^{C_2}(A)$ to $[M,\alpha_M] - [M,-\alpha_M]$.
            \item $\mathbf{2} \circ \mathbf{3} \in \operatorname{End}(\hat{K}_0(A))$ is given by mapping the class of a Fredholm cycle\footnote{see \Cref{defi: fred cycle}.} $(\mathcal{E},F) \in K_0^{\operatorname{Fr}}(A)$ to $(\mathcal{E} \oplus \mathcal{E},F \oplus  -F) \in K_0^{\operatorname{Fr}}(A)$.
            \item When $A$ is inner graded \emph{or} $A$ is complex, then $\mathbb{K}((A \hat\otimes Cl^{0,2})_u) \simeq \mathbb{K}(A_u)$, and the map $\mathbf{4} \circ \mathbf{1} \in \operatorname{End}(K_0(A_u))$ is given by mapping the class of a finitely generated projective $A$-module $[M] \in K_0(A)$ to $[M \oplus M_\alpha] \in K_0(A)$, where $M_\alpha$ has the same underlying abelian group $\underline{M}$ as $M$, and the $A$-action is given by $\underline{m}.a:=\underline{m\alpha_A(a)}.$
            \item Under the same assumption on $A$ as in the last point, the map $\mathbf{1} \circ \mathbf{4} \in \operatorname{End}(K_0^{C_2}(A))$ is given by mapping the class of a $C_2$-equivariant finitely generated projective $A$-module $[M,\alpha_M] \in K_0^{C_2}(A)$ to $[M \oplus M, (m,n) \mapsto (\alpha_M(n),\alpha_M(m))] \in K_0^{C_2}(A)$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
{(Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro)}\label{thm: Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro}
    For every non-negative integer $n$, there is a canonical isomorphism of abelian groups
    \[
    K^{-n}(*) \cong \frac{\{\operatorname{finitely~generated~graded~Cl^{n,0}-modules}\}^{\operatorname{gp}}}{\{\operatorname{finitely~generated~graded~Cl^{n+1,0}-modules}\}^{\operatorname{gp}}}
    \]
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
\hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  A graded complex $C^*$-algebra $(A,\varepsilon)$ is a complex $C^*$-algebra $A$ equipped with a $*$-automorphism $\varepsilon$ such that $\varepsilon^2=1$. $\varepsilon$ is called the grading on $A$. The elements of the $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of $A$ are called even and odd, respectively.
        \item For $G$ a locally compact second countable group, a complex $G$-$C^*$-algebra $(A,\alpha)$ is a $C^*$-algebra $A$ together with a continuous homomorphism $\alpha: G \rightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(A)$, where $\operatorname{Aut(A)}$ is equipped with the point-norm topology.
        \item A Real $C^*$-algebra $(A,\tau)$ is a complex $C^*$-algebra $A$ equipped with a $\mathbb C$-anti-linear $*$-automorphism $\tau$ such that $\tau^2=1$. $\tau$ is called the Real structure on $A$. \footnote{Sometimes, the Real structure will simply be denoted by $a \mapsto \bar{a}$.} The real $C^*$-algebra associated to $(A,\tau)$ is $A_{\tau}:=\{ a \in A \mid a = \tau(a)\}$, and it can be shown that this induces an equivalence of categories between real and Real $C^*$-algebras.
        \item For any two (or all three) of the adjectives defined before, we combine them in the obvious way by requiring the corresponding structure maps to commute.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- notn-1: body_md -->
\label{notn: prelim}
    We follow the following conventions throughout this article.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Unless otherwise mentioned, $G$ will denote a locally compact second countable group. 
        \item As already mentioned in the introduction, we will by default be working be working with Real $C^*$-algebras. Results in the complex case can be deduced by simply ignoring the Real structure. We \emph{do not} mention the word ``Real" unless there is an explicit need to do so.
        \item We denote the category of (ungraded) Real $G$-$C^*$-algebras (with the obvious morphisms) by $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$. This category is enriched over topological spaces using the point-norm topology on the hom sets (see \cite[Section 2.2]{D} for details), and the mapping space is denoted by $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_G(A,B)$. The set of path componentns of $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_G(A,B)$ is denoted by $[A,B]_G$. If it is clear from the context, we suppress the $G$ from the notation.
        \item The symmetric monoidal structures on $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$ will be denoted by $-\otimes_? -$, where $? \in \{\min,\max\}$ corresponds to the minimal and maximal tensor products. If an algebra under consideration is nuclear, we often omit the decoration from the tensor product.
        \item We denote the category of graded, Real $G$-$C^*$-algebras (with the obvious morphisms) by $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$. Its symmetric monoidal structures will be denoted by $-\hat\otimes_? -$, where $? \in \{\min,\max\}$ corresponds to the graded minimal and maximal tensor products. If an algebra under consideration is nuclear, we often omit the decoration from the tensor product (see also \cite[Corollary E.2.19]{WY}). $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$ is also topologically enriched in a way analogous to the ungraded case mentioned above; the only difference being that the desired equivariance now is with respect to $G \times C_2$.
        \item Finally, we remark that in exceptional cases where we do have to work with the category of complex $C^*$-algebras (for example, in \Cref{cor: endomorphisms in the complex graded case}), we keep using the same notation as above. This should not create any confusion.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end notn-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{example: basic examples}
    \hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The base field $\mathbb C$ is trivially graded, and is always equipped with the trivial $G$-action. \emph{In the Real situation, the Real structure on $\mathbb C$ is given by pointwise complex conjugation, and is omitted from the notation}.
        \item The Clifford algebras come with a natural grading, and carry the trivial action of the external group $G$.
        \item $\mathcal{S}:= C_0(\mathbb R)$ with the even-odd grading, trivial $G$-action, and the Real structure given by pointwise complex conjugation is going to be a very important algebra for us. By choosing an odd, increasing homeomorphism between $(-1,1)$ and $\mathbb R$ ({the choice of this homeomorphism does not matter as the space of all such homeomorphisms is contractible}), we obtain an isomorphism between $\mathcal{S}$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$, the \emph{bounded transform} of $\mathcal{S}$. We mention another perspective on $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ below, which comes very handy in concrete situations. Consider the map
        \begin{align*}
    \Phi:\Tilde{\mathcal{S}} &\rightarrow \{f:[0,1) \rightarrow Cl^{0,1} \mid f(0) \in \mathbb{C} \subseteq Cl^{0,1}\} \subseteq C_0([0,1),Cl^{0,1})\\
    f&\mapsto f_{\operatorname{ev}}\mid_{[0,1)} + \varepsilon f_{\operatorname{odd}}\mid_{[0,1)}, 
\end{align*}
where $f_{\operatorname{ev}},f_{\operatorname{odd}}$ denote the even and odd parts of $f$ respectively, and $\varepsilon$ is the non-trivial generator of $Cl^{0,1}$. $\Phi$ can directly be checked to be an isomorphism in $\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$.
        \item A grading on a $C^*$-algebra is said to be \emph{inner} if it is given by conjugation with a self-adjoint unitary in the multiplier algebra of $A$. If $A$ is furthermore equivariant and/or Real, the unitary needs to satisfy the required invariance conditions. The algebras of $G$-continuous bounded and compact operators on a graded $G$-Hilbert space are naturally inner graded. The Clifford algebra $Cl^{p,q}$ is inner graded if $p-q \equiv 0 ~(\operatorname{mod}4)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- notn-2: body_md -->
We denote by $G_2$ the group $G \times C_2$ (equipped with the product topology).
<!-- end notn-2 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
Although the categories $\mathsf G_2\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$ and $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$ are equivalent (by definition!), the symmetric monoidal structures on them are different. See \cite[Section 3.1]{AS} for a categorical perspective on the symmetric monoidal structures on $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
\label{prop: KOC2}
    The following facts about $G$-equivariant $K$-theory are well-known.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  $K_0^G(\mathbb C)$ is a ring with multiplication obtained from the external tensor product of $G$-vector spaces, and is isomorphic to $R(G)$, the representation ring of $G$. In particular, the ring $K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb C)$ is isomorphic to $\frac{\mathbb Z[x]}{x^2=1}$, the group ring of $C_2$. The preferred isomorphism maps the trivial representation of $C_2$ on $\mathbb C$ to $1 \in \frac{\mathbb Z[x]}{x^2=1}$ and the sign representation of $C_2$ on $\mathbb C$ to $x \in \frac{\mathbb Z[x]}{x^2=1}$. 
        \item More generally, the external product with an element of $K^G_0(\mathbb C)$ refines $K^G_n(-)$ to functors \footnote{this should not be confused with the ``$G$-action on $K^G$-groups induced by the action on the algebra", because in general there is no such action! When $G$ is $C_2$, then this action exists, but can be shown to be always trivial.}
        \[
        K_n^G(-): \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg} \rightarrow R(G)\text{-}\operatorname{Mod} \forall~ n \geq 0
        \] 
        \item Of importance to us is the Green-Julg theorem, which asserts that there is a natural isomorphism
        \[
        K^G_n(A) \cong K_n(A \rtimes G) ~\forall~n \geq 0
        \]
        See \cite[Theorem 11.7.1]{BLAK} for a proof. For the case of $G=C_2$, note that we have a natural isomorphism $A \rtimes C_2 \cong (A \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})_u$ (see \cite[Proposition 14.5.1]{BLAK}) and will sometimes use this identification without mentioning.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop: KOC2 CL01}
    $K_n^{C_2}(Cl^{0,1}) \cong K_n(\mathbb C) ~\forall~n \in \mathbb N_{\geq 0} $. The $C_2$-action on $K_n^{C_2}(Cl^{0,1})$ induced by $K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb C)$ (as dictated by \Cref{prop: KOC2}.2) is given by the identity.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We begin by analyzing the maps
    \[
    K_n^{C_2}(\mathbb C) \xrightarrow{\iota_*} K_n^{C_2}(Cl^{0,1}).
    \]
    Consider the commutative diagram (with the unlabeled horizontal arrow us so defined to render the diagram commutative)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{K_n^{C_2}(\mathbb{C})} && {K_n^{C_2}(Cl^{0,1})} \\
	{K_n(Cl^{0,1}_u)} && {K_n(Cl^{0,2}_u) \cong K_n(M_2(\mathbb{C}_u))} \\
	{K_n(\mathbb{C}) \oplus K_n(\mathbb{C})} && {K_n(\mathbb{C})}
	\arrow["{\iota_*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\cong"', no head, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\cong", no head, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{(\iota \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})_u}", from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\cong", from=3-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\cong"', from=3-3, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the top vertical isomorphisms are induced by the Green-Julg theorem, and the lower vertical isomorphisms are induced by the canonical maps. We claim that the bottom horizontal map is given by addition. To that end, one checks that the inclusion $Cl^{0,1} \rightarrow Cl^{0,2}$ corresponds to the homomorphism
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb C \oplus \mathbb C &\rightarrow M_2(\mathbb C)\\
    (x,y) &\mapsto \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
        x+y & x-y \\
        x-y & x+y
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}
under the standard identifications. Precomposing with the two inclusions of $\mathbb C$ into $(\mathbb C \oplus \mathbb C)_u$ therefore induce the homomorphisms $\mathbb C \rightarrow M_2(\mathbb C)_u$ given by 
\[
 \lambda \mapsto \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
        \lambda & \lambda \\ \lambda & \lambda
    \end{pmatrix}  ~~\text{and}~~\mu \mapsto \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
        \mu & -\mu \\ -\mu & \mu
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The two homomorphisms can be homotoped to the left-upper-corner inclusion and/or the right-lower-corner inclusion. The claim now follows from \cite[Lemma 2.7.6]{WY}.

To understand the $C_2$-action on $K_n^{C_2}(Cl^{0,1})$ induced by $K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb C)$, one notes that the flip action on $K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb C)$ is invariant under the addition map, and that $\iota_*$ is an $\mathbb Z[C_2]$-module homomorphism.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{prop: K0C2S}
    $K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S}) \cong \mathbb Z$. The $C_2$-action on $K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S})$ induced by $K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb C)$ is given by $n \mapsto -n$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\footnote{We probably are not giving the cleanest of this result! Instead, we mention in the proof some ideas which we will use later. We are also implicitly identifying $\mathcal{S}$ with the bounded transform $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ in this proof.}
Consider the diagram in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn: mapping cone for s}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	{\ker(\operatorname{ev}_1)} & {\{f:[0,1] \rightarrow Cl^{0,1} \mid f(0) \in \mathbb{C} \subseteq Cl^{0,1}\}} & {C([0,1],Cl^{0,1})} \\
	{\tilde{\mathcal{S}}} & {\mathbb{C}} & {Cl^{0,1}}
	\arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\Phi, \cong}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{ev_0}, \simeq}"', two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{ev}_1}"{description}, dashed, two heads, from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{ev_0}, \simeq}"', two heads, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{ev_0}}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\iota"', from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
where $\Phi$ is as in \Cref{example: basic examples}.3. Note that the right square is a pullback square (it is the defining square of the mapping cylinder construction; see also \Cref{example: mapping cone sequence is Schochet}.2), and the left square as well as the two triangles involving the dashed edge commute up to homotopy. The rest follows by applying the $K_0^{C_2}(-)$ functor to \Cref{eqn: mapping cone for s}, using the homotopy invariance and exicision properties of equivariant $K$-theory and the proof of \Cref{prop: KOC2 CL01}. Observe that the kernel of the addition map $\mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z \rightarrow \mathbb Z$ is
    $
    \{(n,-n) \mid n \in \mathbb Z\},
    $
    which is evidently isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$ with the action $n \mapsto -n$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a separable $G$-$C^*$-algebra. Set $QA:= A *A$, the coproduct in the category of separable $G$-$C^*$-algebras. Denote by $qA$ the kernel of the fold map $QA \rightarrow A$. $qA$ gets a natural $G$-action from $A$.
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
\label{rem: qA properties}
    The following remarks about $qA$ are in order.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $qA$ fits in a short exact sequence
        \[
        0 \rightarrow qA \rightarrow QA \rightarrow A \rightarrow 0.
        \]
        The sequence splits in two canonical ways, depending on embedding $A$ into one of the components of $QA$.
        \item The $q$ construction is functorial, and there are two natural maps $qA \rightarrow A$ given by restricting the homomorphisms
        \[
        A * A \xrightarrow{(1_A,0)} A, ~~~~ A * A \xrightarrow{(0,1_A)} A
        \]
        to $qA$.
        \item Given $A,B \in \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$, a prequasi-homomorphism from $A$ to $B$ consists of a $G$-$C^*$-algebra $E$, two $G$-equivariant $*$-homomorphisms\footnote{$\overline{\alpha}$ should not be confused with any sort of complex conjugation!} $\alpha,\overline{\alpha}:A \rightarrow E$, an ideal $J \triangleleft E$, and a $G$-equivariant $*$-homomorphism $\mu:J\rightarrow B$ such that $\alpha(x)-\overline{\alpha}(x) \in J~\forall~x\in A$. We write it as
    \[
                                                                                                                                                                                                         
\begin{tikzcd}
	{A } & {E \triangleright J} & B
	\arrow["{\overline{\alpha}}"', from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\alpha", shift left=3, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\mu", from=1-2, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}
    \]
    By universal properties, a prequasi-homomorphism $A \rightarrow B$ yields a map $\mu \circ q(\alpha,\overline{\alpha}):qA \rightarrow B$, which we simply denote by $\alpha-\overline{\alpha}$.
        \item When $A=\mathbb C$, there is a concrete description of $q\mathbb C$:
        \[
        q\mathbb C \cong \{f\in C_0((0,1],M_2(\mathbb C)) \mid f(1) ~\text{is diagonal}\}.
        \]
        This is stated in \cite[Exercise 10.11.13.g]{BLAK}, and a proof with a lot of details and other background is available in \cite{SAARBRUCKEN}. Technically, loc.\! cit.\! gives a concrete function algebra description of the universal unital $C^*$-algebra on two projections, from which our result can be directly deduced in light of the defining short exact sequence of $q\mathbb C$ as mentioned in the first remark above. See also \cite[Section 6]{CUNSURVEY}.
        \item The above isomorphism directly shows that, in light of \Cref{example: basic examples}.3, \[\mathcal{S} \rtimes C_2 \cong (\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})_u \cong q\mathbb C.\] This bridges the gap between the spectral model (studied in the next subsection) and the Cuntz picture. In particular, the proof of the next proposition can also be deduced from \Cref{thm: spectral model of g eq k theory} in light of a restriction-coinduction adjunction at the level of the compact-stabilized homotopy categories. Similar ideas are used in the proof of \Cref{lem: qC special}.
        \item An important technical feature of $q\mathbb{C}$ is \emph{semi-projectivity}, which implies that for all $A \in \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$, the canonical map
        \[
        [q\mathbb{C},A]_G \xrightarrow{\cong} [[q\mathbb{C},A]]_G
        \]
        from the $G$-equivariant homotopy classes of maps to the $G$-equivariant asymptotic homotopy classes of maps from $q\mathbb{C}$ to $A$ is a bijection of sets. See \cite[Exercise 4.7.1, Proposition 25.1.7]{BLAK} and \cite{Blackadar1985Shape} for general results on semi-projective $C^*$-algebras. The proof of $q\mathbb{C}$ being semi-projective is the content of \cite[Theorem 7]{Loring2008Projective}.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop: Cuntz picture k-theory}
    Let $G$ be a compact group and $A$ a $G$-$C^*$-algebra. Then, there is a natural isomorphism of abelian groups
    \[
    [q\mathbb C,A \otimes \mathcal{K}(L^2G_\mathbb N)]_G \cong K_0^{G}(A).
    \]
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The result is well known, see for example \cite[Section 17.6]{BLAK}, \cite[Remark 1]{CUNTZ2}. The compact group action (and the Real structure) do not cause any extra difficulty as $G$-equivariant\footnote{$G$-equivariant adjointable operators are precisely the $G$-fixed points of the $G$-$C^*$-algebra of adjointable operators on a $G$-Hilbert module.}, $G$-continuous Fredholm operators on $G$-Hilbert modules classify $G$-equivariant $K_0$ when $G$ is compact; see \Cref{thm: spectral model of g eq k theory}.5 for example.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
\label{rem: the map in the cuntz picture iso}
     We mention that the isomorphism \begin{align}\label{eqn: cuntz picture dia}
        K_0^G(A) &\xrightarrow{\cong} [q\mathbb C,A \otimes \mathcal{K}(L^2G_\mathbb N)]_G
    \end{align}
    is given by precomposition with the first map $q\mathbb C \rightarrow \mathbb C$ as described in \Cref{rem: qA properties}.2, see \cite[Exercise 10.11.13.f]{BLAK}. By taking $n$-fold loops on both sides of \Cref{eqn: cuntz picture dia}, we obtain 
    \[
    K_n^G(A) \cong \pi_n(\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_G(q\mathbb C,A \otimes \mathcal{K}(L^2G_\mathbb N)))
    \]
    for all $n \in \mathbb N$.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop: KOC2S to KOC2C commutes}
    The homomorphism $\mathbb Z \rightarrow K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S})$ given by $1 \mapsto p_1-p_2$ renders the diagram 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S})} && {K_0^{C_2}(\mathbb{C})} \\
	\mathbb Z && {\mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z}
	\arrow["{{\operatorname{ev}_0}_*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\cong", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["{n \mapsto (n,-n)}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
commutative, where the right isomorphism is the isomorphism described in \Cref{prop: KOC2}.1.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From the descriptions of $p_1$ and $p_2$ and \Cref{rem: the map in the cuntz picture iso}, it is clear that $\operatorname{ev}_0(p_1-p_2)$ corresponds to the map $q\mathbb C \rightarrow M_2$ given by the difference of the $C_2$-equivariant projections $\begin{pmatrix}
        1 & 0 \\
        0 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0\\
        0 & 1
    \end{pmatrix}$ in $M_2$. Now, $M_2$ with the diagonal-off diagonal grading is nothing but the algebra of operators on the $C_2$-vector space $\mathbb C^{\operatorname{triv}} \oplus \mathbb C^{\operatorname{sign}}$. The rest follows directly.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
The left vertical arrow above is in fact an isomorphism. We declare $p:=p_1-p_2$ to be the preferred generator of $K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S}) \cong \mathbb Z$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since we know that $K_0^{C_2}(\mathcal{S})$ is abstractly isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, this follows from the elementary observation that the map \[
    \mathbb Z \xrightarrow{n \mapsto (n,-n)} \mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z
    \]
    can only factor through $\mathbb Z$ (in the category of abelian groups) through an isomorphism $\mathbb Z \rightarrow \mathbb Z$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
Let $A \in \mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$.  Define the $G$-equivariant spectral $K$-theory space of $A$, denoted $\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)$, to be 
    \[
    \mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A):=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{G_2}(\mathcal{S},A \hat\otimes \hat{\mathcal{K}}_G),
    \]
    the $G \times C_2$-equivariant $*$-homomorphisms from $\mathcal{S}$ to $A \hat\otimes \hat{\mathcal{K}}_G$ equipped with the point-norm topology.
   We define the spectral $K$-theory groups of $A$ to be the homotopy groups of $\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)$,
    \[
    K_n^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A):=\pi_n(\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A),\underline{0})
    \]
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
\label{defi: fred cycle}
    Let $A \in \mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item A $G$-Fredholm cycle over $A$ is a tuple $(\mathcal{E},F)$, where $\mathcal{E}$ is a graded, countably generated Hilbert $A,G$-module \footnote{see \cite[Section 2.1]{MEYER} for the definition}, and $F$ is a $G$-continuous, $G$-invariant, odd, self-adjoint Fredholm operator on it.
        \item Two $G$-Fredholm cycles $(\mathcal{E}_0,F_0)$ and $(\mathcal{E}_1,F_1)$ over $A$ are said to be \emph{concordant} if there exists a $G$-Fredholm cycle $(\mathcal{E},F)$ over $A \hat\otimes C[0,1]\cong C([0,1],A)$ such that $(\mathcal{E} \hat\otimes_{\operatorname{ev}_i}A, \operatorname{ev}_i(F)) \cong (\mathcal{E}_i,F_i)$ for $i=0,1$, where $\operatorname{ev}_t:C([0,1],A) \rightarrow A$ is the homomorphism given by $\operatorname{ev}_t(f)=f(t)$.
        \item Denote by $K_0^{G,\operatorname{Fr}}(A)$ the abelian monoid of concordance classes of $G$-Fredholm cycles over $A$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm: spectral model of g eq k theory}
    Some key features of the spectral model and the Fredholm model of graded, $G$-equivariant $K$-theory are mentioned below. In what follows, $A,B,...$ denote arbitrary graded $G$-$C^*$-algebras, and all the morphisms are in the category $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)$ is an $H$-group. Consequently, all the equivariant spectral $K$-groups are in fact abelian groups.
        \item A short exact sequence $0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow 0$ in $\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$ yields a Serre fibration on the associated spectral $K$-theory spaces.
        \item The functors $K_n^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(-): \mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg} \rightarrow \operatorname{Ab}$ preserve filtered colimits for all $n \in \mathbb N_{\geq 0}$.
        \item The functors 
        \[
        K_0^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(-): (\mathsf G\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg},\hat\otimes_!) \rightarrow (\operatorname{Ab},\otimes)
        \]
        are lax monoidal.
        \item We have a natural isomorphism of abelian groups \[\pi_0(\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)) \xrightarrow{\cong} K_0^{G,\operatorname{Fr}}(A).\]
        \item When $A$ is inner graded, we have a natural isomorphism of abelian groups
        \[
        \pi_n(\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)) \cong K_n^{G}(A) ~\forall~n \geq 0.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Assertion 1 follows from the more general statement that given a graded morphism $\varphi : \mathcal{S} \rightarrow A$, the induced morphism
    \[
    \mathcal{S} \rightarrow A \hat\otimes M_2(\mathbb C) = M_2(A), ~~~ f \mapsto \begin{pmatrix}
        \varphi(f) & 0\\
        0 & \alpha(\varphi(f))
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]
    is nullhomotopic in $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_G(\mathcal{S},A \hat\otimes M_2(\mathbb C))$ (here $\alpha$ is the grading on $A$), where $M_2(\mathbb C)$ has the grading given by $\operatorname{Ad}(\tau)$, where $\tau=\begin{pmatrix}
        1 & 0 \\
        0 & -1
    \end{pmatrix}$. See \cite[Remark 1.7]{HG}.\\\\
    Assertion 2 follows from the non-equivariant assertion proven in \cite[Section 3.2]{D} by taking $G$-fixed points. Note that taking $G$-fixed points is an exact functor because $G$ is compact.\\\\
    By similar reductions as done before, to show Assertion 3, it suffices to prove that for a filtered diagram $(A_i)_{i \in I}$ of non-equivariant graded $C^*$-algebras with colimit $A$, one has a weak homotopy equivalence of spaces
    \[
    \operatorname{colim}_{i \in I} \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal{S},A_i) \rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal{S},A).
    \]
    Upon passing to the Cayley transform picture (see \cite[Lemma 3.1]{D}), the result follows from \cite[Corollary to Theorem 12]{PALAIS}.\\\\
    The key to demonstrating Assertion 4 is the comultiplication map on $\mathcal{S}$ as described in \cite[Section 4.2]{D}. The details are in \cite[Section 6]{D}, and the same proofs go through equivariantly. See also \Cref{cor: s cocommutative coalgebra}.\\\\
    We now discuss Assertion 5. A natural map $\pi_0(\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)) \xrightarrow{\cong} K_0^{G,\operatorname{Fr}}(A)$ can be written by directly emulating the non-equivariant construction as in \cite[Section 8.5]{D}. We mention some aspects of it for ease of reference later.

    Firstly, we implicitly replace $\mathcal{S}$ with $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$, and the Fredholm cycles with essentially unitary ones. Recall that \[A \hat\otimes \hat{\mathcal{K}}_G \cong \mathcal{K}_A(A \otimes \widehat{L^2G_{\mathbb N}}),\footnote{we do not decorate the tensor product of two graded Hilbert modules, since no Koszul signs are involved as there are no multiplicative structures.}\] the $G$-equivariant graded $C^*$-algebra of $A$-compact operators on the standard graded $G$-equivariant Hilbert $A$-module. Given $\varphi: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow A \hat\otimes \hat{\mathcal{K}}_G \cong \mathcal{K}_A(A \otimes \widehat{L^2G_{\mathbb N}})$, set \[\mathcal{H}_{\varphi}:=\overline{\varphi(\mathcal{S})(A \otimes \widehat{L^2G_{\mathbb N}})},\] and note that $\varphi$ restricts to a non-degenerate homomorphism
    \[
    \varphi^{\operatorname{nd}}: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_A(\mathcal{H}_\varphi).
    \]
    The crucial point here is that $\varphi^{\operatorname{nd}}$ indeed maps to the $A$-compact operators on the (not necessarily complementable) submodule $\mathcal{H}_\varphi \subseteq A \otimes \widehat{L^2G_{\mathbb N}}$, as is guaranteed by \cite[Lemma 4.1]{MEYER}. Non-degeneracy of $\varphi^{\operatorname{nd}}$ implies that there exists a unique $G$-equivariant, graded homomorphism $\tilde{\varphi}: C[-1,1] \rightarrow \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\varphi})$ extending $\varphi^{\operatorname{nd}}$. The natural map is now given by 
    \begin{align*}
       \pi_0(\mathbb{K}^{G,\operatorname{sp}}(A)) \xrightarrow{}& K_0^{G,\operatorname{Fr}}(A)  \\
       \varphi \longmapsto& (\mathcal{H}_\varphi,\tilde{\varphi}(x))
    \end{align*}
    The proof that this map is bijective now follows with the obvious modifications from \cite[Section 8.5]{D}.\\\\
    Finally, we come to Assertion 6. We just discuss the case of $\pi_0$ when $A$ is unital and ungraded, the general case follows from the techniques described in \cite[Section 2.9]{WY}. One proof strategy in the unital, ungraded case would be to show that the natural map $K_0^G(A) \rightarrow K_0^{G,\operatorname{Fr}}(A)$ has an inverse given by taking the $G$-equivariant index of $G$-invariant Fredholm operators (as done in the non-equivariant case in \cite[Section 8.4]{D}), and then conclude by Assertion 5. However, granted the results of loc.\! cit.\! and the Green-Julg theorem, we can quickly obtain the conclusion by leveraging the fact that $A \rtimes G \cong (A \otimes \mathcal{K}(L^2G))^G$, as shown in \cite[Proposition 11.2]{HGT}. See also the proof of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{DEKM}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- notn-3: body_md -->
Having established natural isomorphisms between different models of graded $K$-theory, we henceforth denote the $G$-equivariant graded $K$-groups as $\hat{K}^G_*(-)$.
<!-- end notn-3 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop: omnibus graded k-theory}
\hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There is a short exact sequence
        \[
        0 \xrightarrow{} C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \xrightarrow{\psi} \mathcal{S} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_0} \mathbb C \rightarrow 0
        \]
        in $\widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$.
        \item For every $A \in \widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$, the map
        \[
        \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes A) \xrightarrow{(\operatorname{ev}_0 \hat\otimes 1_A)_*} \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal{S},A)
        \]
        have natural continuous sections $\sigma_A$. Furthermore, $\sigma_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{ev}_0)=\operatorname{1}_{\mathcal{S}}$.
        \item For every $A \in \widehat{\mathsf C}^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$, we have naturally split exact sequences
        \[
        0\rightarrow \hat{K}_*(C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \hat\otimes A) \xrightarrow{\psi_*} \hat{K}_*(\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes A) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{{ev}_0}_*} \hat{K}_*(A) \rightarrow 0.
        \]
        \item For each $n \in \mathbb N$, multiplication by the Bott class $[\beta_\mathbb C^n] \in \hat{K}(C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n})$ yields natural isomorphisms 
        \[
        \hat{K}_*(A) \rightarrow \hat{K}_*(C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n} \hat\otimes A).
        \] In particular, $\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}) \cong \mathbb Z$, and the isomorphism identifies $[\beta_{\mathbb C}^n]$ and $1$. The grading $\alpha$ on $C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}$ induces the map $(-1)^n: \mathbb Z \rightarrow \mathbb Z$. 
        \item $\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S}) \cong \mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z$ as abelian groups, with the preferred isomorphism mapping $\psi_*[\beta_\mathbb C]=:u$ to $(0,1)$ and $[\operatorname{1_\mathcal{S}}]=:e$ to $(1,0)$.
        \item The composition
        \[
        C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \xrightarrow{\psi} \mathcal{S} \xrightarrow{\beta_\mathbb C} C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} 
        \]
        induces multiplication by $2$ on $\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} ) \cong \mathbb Z$.
        \item In the context of Assertion 5, we have $\alpha_*(u)=-u$ and $\alpha_*(e)=e-u$, where $\alpha$ denotes the grading on $\mathcal{S}$.
        \item There exists an isomorphism of $C_2$-abelian groups between $\hat{K_0}(\mathcal{S})$ and $\mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z$ with the flip action, with the preferred isomorphism sending $[1_\mathcal{S}]$ to $(1,0)$ and $[\alpha_\mathcal{S}]$ to $(0,1)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We begin with Assertion 1. Consider 
    \[
     0 \xrightarrow{} J\xrightarrow{} \mathcal{S} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_0} \mathbb C \rightarrow 0
    \]
    where $J:=\ker(\operatorname{ev}_0)$. Then, we have 
    \begin{align}\label{eqn: J and C0 0 inf}
        J \xrightarrow{\cong} C_0((0,\infty)) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} ~~~~~~~~~~~~~f \mapsto f_{\operatorname{ev}}\mid_{(0,\infty)}\hat\otimes 1+f_{\operatorname{odd}}\mid_{(0,\infty)}\hat\otimes \varepsilon,
    \end{align}
    where $f_{\operatorname{ev}}(x)=\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}, f_{{\operatorname{odd}}}(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}$, and $\varepsilon$ is the canonical generator of $Cl^{0,1}$. Take a homeomorphism $h:(0,\infty) \rightarrow \mathbb R$ such that \[\lim_{t \to 0} h(t)=-\infty, \lim_{t \to \infty} h(t)=\infty.\]
    For concreteness, take $h(x)=\ln(x)$. We can define our sought after map $\psi:C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \rightarrow \mathcal{S}$ using $h$ and the isomorphism above.\\\\
    For Assertion 2, note that a direct calculation using the generators $e^{-x^2}$ and $xe^{-x^2}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ shows that the composite
    \[
    \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},A) \xrightarrow{1_{\mathcal{S}} \hat\otimes -} \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes \mathcal{S},\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes A) \xrightarrow{\Delta^*} \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S} \hat\otimes A) \xrightarrow{(\operatorname{ev}_0 \hat\otimes 1_A)_*} \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},A)
    \]
    is the identity, and has the required effect on $\operatorname{ev}_0 \in \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},\mathbb C)$ too.\\\\
    Assertion 3 follows immediately from Assertion 2.\\\\
    We just prove the last part of Assertion 4, since the first two parts are the content of \cite[Section 9]{D}. Recall that the Bott class is the class in graded $K$-theory represented by the Bott map, which is the functional calculus of the embedding of $\mathbb R^{n}$ in ${Cl^{0,n}}$ as a homomorphism $\mathcal{S} \rightarrow C_0(\mathbb R^{n},Cl^{0,n})$.\footnote{strictly speaking, we mean $\mathbb R^{0,n}$ here}
    
    We begin with the case $n=1$. To simplify the notation, we denote $\beta_\mathbb C^1$ by $\beta_\mathbb C$. We have to show that $\alpha_*([\beta_{\mathbb C}])=-[\beta_{\mathbb C}]$.  By definition of $\beta_{\mathbb C}$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \beta_{\mathbb C}: \mathcal{S} &\rightarrow C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \cong C_0(\mathbb R,Cl^{0,1})~~~~~
    f \mapsto t \mapsto f(t\varepsilon).
    \end{align*}
    This is same as the map $f \mapsto f^{\operatorname{ev}}+f^{\operatorname{odd}}\varepsilon$, as can be readily checked on the generators $u$ and $v$ of $\mathcal{S}$. Therefore, we have \begin{align*}
        \alpha \circ \beta_\mathbb{C} : \mathcal{S} &\rightarrow C_0(\mathbb R,Cl^{0,1}),~~~~~f \mapsto f^{\operatorname{ev}}-f^{\operatorname{odd}}\varepsilon.
    \end{align*}
    We now identify 
    \[
    \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} ) \cong \operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb R^{+},\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1})).
    \]
    Furthermore, under the Cayley transform isomorphism, we have a homeomorphism\footnote{in what follows, we denote by $\mathbb R^+$ the one-point compactification of $\mathbb R$. $\infty \in \mathbb R^+$ is the point at infinity.}
    \begin{align} \label{eqn: iso Rplus and hom s cl01}
        \mathbb R^+ &\rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1}) \\
        \infty &\mapsto 0 \\
        t &\longmapsto f \mapsto f^{\operatorname{ev}}(t)+f^{\operatorname{odd}}(t)\varepsilon
    \end{align}
    Whence, we have a homeomorphism of spaces
    \[
     \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} ) \cong \operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb R^+,\mathbb R^+),
    \]
    under which $\beta_{\mathbb C}$ corresponds to the identity, and $\alpha \circ \beta$ corresponds to the negative of identity. Since degree of the negative identity as a map from $\mathbb R^+$ to itself is $-1$, the conclusion follows.
    
    For the general case, we consider the commutative diagram of abelian groups (see \cite[Section 7.1]{D} for the details)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \otimes &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \otimes\cdots\otimes &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \longrightarrow &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R^n)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}\right)
\\[1ex]
\downarrow\!{\scriptstyle\alpha_*}
&&
\downarrow\!{\scriptstyle\alpha_*}
&&
\downarrow\!{\scriptstyle\alpha_*}
&&
\downarrow\!{\scriptstyle\alpha_*}
\\[1ex]
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \otimes &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \otimes\cdots\otimes &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}\right)
& \longrightarrow &
\hat{K}_0\!\left(C_0(\mathbb R^n)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}\right).
\end{array}
\]
    From \cite[Lemma 9.3.4]{WY} on the one hand we get \[[\beta_\mathbb C]\times [\beta_\mathbb C]\times... \times [\beta_\mathbb C] \mapsto [\beta_\mathbb C^n]\in \hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}).\]
    Since $\alpha_*([\beta_\mathbb C])=-[\beta_\mathbb C]$ for the case dealt with above, from the commutativity of the above diagram, we get on the other hand
    \[
    (-[\beta_\mathbb C])\times (-[\beta_\mathbb C])\times... \times (-[\beta_\mathbb C]) \mapsto \alpha_*[\beta_\mathbb C^n]\in \hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R^n) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,n}).
    \]
    This proves Assertion 4.
    \\\\
    Assertion 5 follows immediately from  Assertions 3 and 4.\\\\
    We now show Assertion 6. Choose a homeomorphism $h:(0,\infty) \rightarrow \mathbb R$ as in the proof of Assertion 1. By definition, the composition $\beta_\mathbb C \circ \psi$ is
    \[
    C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \xrightarrow{h^*} C_0((0,\infty)) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} \xrightarrow{} \mathcal{S} \xrightarrow{\beta_\mathbb C} C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1},
    \]
    where the unlabelled arrow sends 
    \[
    f \hat\otimes 1 \longmapsto x \mapsto f(|x|), ~~~~~~~~f \hat\otimes \varepsilon \longmapsto x \mapsto s(x)f(|x|),
    \]
    where $s(x): \mathbb R \setminus \{0\} \rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ is the sign function\footnote{strictly speaking these are the formulae when $x \neq 0$. At $x=0$ we by default assign the value $0$. We also do this at certain places later without explicitly mentioning.} (this function is nothing but the inverse to the isomorphism in \Cref{eqn: J and C0 0 inf} postcomposed with the inclusion of $J$ into $\mathcal{S}$). The whole composite therefore sends
    \[
    f \hat\otimes 1 \longmapsto f \circ h \circ |\cdot| \hat\otimes 1,~~~~~~~~ f \hat\otimes \varepsilon \longmapsto (s\cdot f\circ h \circ |\cdot|) \hat\otimes \varepsilon.
    \]
    From the description of the Bott map as in the proof of Assertion 4, the induced map
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1}) &\xrightarrow{(\beta_{\mathbb{C}}\circ \psi)_*}  \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})
    \end{align*}
    sends the Bott map to the homomorphism \[
    (f \longmapsto f^{\operatorname{ev}} \circ h \circ |\cdot|)\hat\otimes 1 + (s\cdot f^{\operatorname{odd}}\circ h \circ |\cdot|)\hat\otimes \varepsilon.
    \]
    Upon identifying 
    \[
     \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1} ) \cong \operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb R^{+},\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1})),
    \]
    the Bott map therefore gets mapped to 
    \[
    x \longmapsto f\mapsto (f^{\operatorname{ev}}(h(|x|))\cdot 1+s(x)f^{\operatorname{odd}}(h(|x|))\cdot\varepsilon).
    \]
    But this is same as the function
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb R^+ &\rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1}) \\
        x &\longmapsto f \mapsto \begin{cases}
            f^{\operatorname{ev}}(h(x))\cdot1+f^{\operatorname{odd}}(h(x))\cdot\varepsilon~~~~~~~~~\text{if}~x>0\\
            f^{\operatorname{ev}}(h(-x))\cdot1-f^{\operatorname{odd}}(h(-x))\cdot\varepsilon ~~~~ \text{if}~x<0 \\
            0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ \text{if}~ x=0,\infty
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    Under the identification 
    \[
    \mathbb R^+ \cong \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1})
    \]
    from \Cref{eqn: iso Rplus and hom s cl01},  this corresponds to the function
    \begin{align*}
        h':\mathbb R^+ &\rightarrow \mathbb R^+ \\
        x &\mapsto \begin{cases}
            h(x)~\text{if}~x > 0\\
            -h(-x)~\text{if}~x < 0 \\
            \infty~~~~~~\text{if} ~x=0,\infty
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    The {local degree formula} yields that the degree of $h'$ is $2$. The proof is now completed by the following argument: consider the diagram
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb{R},Cl^{0,1}))} && {\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},C_0(\mathbb{R},Cl^{0,1}))} \\
	{\operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb{R}^+,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1}))} && {\operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb{R}^+,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S},Cl^{0,1}))} \\
	{\operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb{R}^+,\mathbb{R}^+)} && {\operatorname{Map}_*(\mathbb{R}^+,\mathbb{R}^+)}
	\arrow["{(\beta_{\mathbb{C}} \circ \psi)_*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\cong", no head, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\cong", no head, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\cong", no head, from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["\cong", no head, from=2-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3],
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the bottom horizontal arrow is defined so as to make the diagram commute. Therefore the bottom horizontal arrow sends 
\[
\operatorname{id}: \mathbb R^+ \rightarrow \mathbb R^+ 
\]
to
\[
h':\mathbb R^+ \rightarrow \mathbb R^+,
\]
since we showed above that the right-down itinerary maps $\beta_\mathbb C$ to $h'$, and the left vertical composite identifies $\beta_\mathbb C$ and $\operatorname{id}$, as was observed in the proof of Assertion 4. Thus, the map induced by $\beta_\mathbb C \circ \psi$ on $\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R,Cl^{0,1}))$ is multiplication by the degree of $h'$, which is equal to $2$.
\\\\
For Assertion 7, we consider the commutative diagram (we denote by $\alpha$ the grading on the respective algebras)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	0 && 0 \\
	{\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})} && {\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R)\hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})} \\
	{\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})} && {\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})} \\
	{\hat{K_0}(\mathbb{C})} && {\hat{K}_0(\mathbb{C})} \\
	0 && 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\alpha_*=-1.}", from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\psi_*}", from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["{\psi_*}", from=2-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["{\alpha_*}", from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["{{\operatorname{ev}_0}_*}", from=3-1, to=4-1]
	\arrow["{{\operatorname{ev}_0}_*}", from=3-3, to=4-3]
	\arrow["{\alpha_*=1.}", from=4-1, to=4-3]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=5-1]
	\arrow[from=4-3, to=5-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the the top horizontal map is negation from Assertion 4, and the bottom horizontal map is the identity since $\mathbb C$ has the trivial grading. The commutativity of the top rectangle yields that \[\alpha_*(u)=-u.\]
Understanding $\alpha_*(e)$ takes a bit more work. From Assertion 5 and the commutativity of the lower rectangle in the above diagram, we can say that 
\[
\alpha_*(e)=e+nu
\]
for some $n \in \mathbb Z$. To compute the value of $n$, we consider the commutative diagram 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})} && {\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})} \\
	{\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb{R}) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})} && {\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb{R}) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})}
	\arrow["{\alpha_*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\beta_*}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\beta_*}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\alpha_*=-1.}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
From Assertion 4 and Assertion 6, we can say that $\beta_*(e)=[\beta_\mathbb C]$ and $\beta_*(u)=2[\beta_\mathbb C]$. Tracing the fate of $e$ under the two itineraries from $\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})$ to $\hat{K}_0(C_0(\mathbb R) \hat\otimes Cl^{0,1})$, we obtain the equation
\[
[\beta_\mathbb C] + 2n\cdot[\beta_\mathbb C]=-[\beta_\mathbb C],
\]
which shows \[n=-1.\] This finishes the proof of Assertion 7.
\\\\
To prove Assertion 8, we note that Assertion 7 shows (in light of Assertion 5) that $(e,\alpha_*e)$ is also a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\hat{K}_0(\mathcal{S})$, and the grading $\alpha_\mathcal{S}$ evidently swaps the basis elements.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
\hfill
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Two maps $f_0,f_1:A \rightarrow B$ in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ are said to be homotopic if there exists a morphism $F:A \rightarrow C([0,1],B)$ such that $\operatorname{ev}_i \circ F=f_i$ for $i=0,1$.
    \item  Let $f:A \rightarrow B$ be a morphism in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$. $f$ is said to be a homotopy equivalence if there exists a morphism $g: B \rightarrow A$ in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ such that the two composites are homotopic to the respective identity maps.
\end{enumerate}
We denote by $\mathcal{W}_h$ the (essentially small) class of homotopy equivalences in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$.
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- defi-6: body_md -->
Denote by ${\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}}$ the Dwyer-Kan localization of $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ at $\mathcal{W}_h$, and denote by \[
    L_h: \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}
    \]
    the localization functor.
<!-- end defi-6 -->
<!-- defi-7: body_md -->
\hfill
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A morphism $f: A \rightarrow B$ in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is said to be a \emph{Schochet fibration} if for all $D \in \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$, the induced map of topological spaces
    \[
    \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(D,A) \xrightarrow{f_*} \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(D,B)
    \]
    is a Serre fibration.
    \item A cartesian square in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ 
                                                                                                                                 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	A & B \\
	D & C
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["f", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
is called \emph{Schochet fibrant} if $f$ is a Schochet fibration.
\item For an $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$, a functor $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}$ will be called \emph{Schochet exact} if it maps Schochet fibrant cartesian squares to cartesian squares.  We denote by 
\[
\mathbf{Fun}^{Sch}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})
\]
the full subcategory of $\mathbf{Fun}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})$ spanned by functors which are Schochet exact.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{example}\label{example: mapping cone sequence is Schochet}
We present a few important examples of Schochet fibrations which will be required later on. For proofs see the relevant sections in \cite{SCHOCHETFIB} and \cite{KKandE}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For any $C^*$-algebra $A$, the canonical map $C([0,1],A) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_0} A$ is a Schochet fibration (and a homotopy equivalence). $C([0,1],A)$ is also called the \emph{path algebra} of $A$, and denoted $PA$.
    \item Pullback of a Schochet fibration along any $*$-homomorphism is a Schochet fibration. Given a $*$-homomorphism $f:B \rightarrow
     C$, denote by $Z(f)$ the pullback $B \times_C PC$. $Z(f)$ is called the \emph{mapping cylinder} of $f$, and the canonical map $Z(f) \rightarrow B$ is a Schochet fibration (and a homotopy equivalence).

     Concretely, we have 
     \[
     Z(f)=\{(b,\gamma) \mid b \in B, \gamma \in PC, \gamma(0)=f(b)\}.
     \]
     There is also a canonical map $\operatorname{ev}_1:Z(f) \rightarrow C$ which is also a Schochet fibration. By definition, the \emph{mapping cone} of $f$ fits in the short exact sequence
     \[
     0 \rightarrow C(f) \rightarrow Z(f) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_1} C \rightarrow 0.
     \]
     This sequence is furthermore semi-split and is called the mapping cone sequence. It will be extremely important for us in Section 3.3.
     
     In the special case that $f$ is an inclusion, $Z(f)$ is isomorphic to all paths in $C$ which start at $B$.
    \item The maximal tensor product with an auxilliary algebra of a Schochet fibrant cartesian square remains a Schochet fibrant cartesian square. The minimal tensor product with an auxilliary algebra of of a mapping cone sequence remains a mapping cone sequence.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}
<!-- end defi-7 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{example: mapping cone sequence is Schochet}
We present a few important examples of Schochet fibrations which will be required later on. For proofs see the relevant sections in \cite{SCHOCHETFIB} and \cite{KKandE}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For any $C^*$-algebra $A$, the canonical map $C([0,1],A) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_0} A$ is a Schochet fibration (and a homotopy equivalence). $C([0,1],A)$ is also called the \emph{path algebra} of $A$, and denoted $PA$.
    \item Pullback of a Schochet fibration along any $*$-homomorphism is a Schochet fibration. Given a $*$-homomorphism $f:B \rightarrow
     C$, denote by $Z(f)$ the pullback $B \times_C PC$. $Z(f)$ is called the \emph{mapping cylinder} of $f$, and the canonical map $Z(f) \rightarrow B$ is a Schochet fibration (and a homotopy equivalence).

     Concretely, we have 
     \[
     Z(f)=\{(b,\gamma) \mid b \in B, \gamma \in PC, \gamma(0)=f(b)\}.
     \]
     There is also a canonical map $\operatorname{ev}_1:Z(f) \rightarrow C$ which is also a Schochet fibration. By definition, the \emph{mapping cone} of $f$ fits in the short exact sequence
     \[
     0 \rightarrow C(f) \rightarrow Z(f) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_1} C \rightarrow 0.
     \]
     This sequence is furthermore semi-split and is called the mapping cone sequence. It will be extremely important for us in Section 3.3.
     
     In the special case that $f$ is an inclusion, $Z(f)$ is isomorphic to all paths in $C$ which start at $B$.
    \item The maximal tensor product with an auxilliary algebra of a Schochet fibrant cartesian square remains a Schochet fibrant cartesian square. The minimal tensor product with an auxilliary algebra of of a mapping cone sequence remains a mapping cone sequence.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop: RALGseph omnibus}
    \hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $\infty$-category $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is locally small, and is canonically equivalent to the $\infty$-category presented by the Kan-enriched\footnote{we implicitly always view a topologically enriched category as a Kan enriched category} category $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$, i.e., by taking its homotopy coherent nerve.
        \item $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is pointed and $L_h$ is reduced, i.e. maps the zero algebra to the zero object in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$.
        \item $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ has finite limits and countable coproducts. $L_h$ preserves finite products and countable coproducts. 
        \item For every left-exact $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$, the equivalence in \Cref{eqn: uni prop ralgseph} restricts to an equivalence 
        \[
        \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex}}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_h^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{h,Sch}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}),
        \]
        where the left-hand entity denotes the full subcategory of $\mathbf{Fun}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})$ spanned by left-exact functors.
        \item $L_h: \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ has a symmetric monoidal refinement for both the minimal and maximal tensor products on $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Moreover, the functors \[\otimes_?:\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \times \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}\] are bi-left exact for $? \in \{\operatorname{min,max}\}$.
        \item For every left-exact and symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$ and $? \in \{\min,\max\}$, the pullback along the symmetric monoidal refinement of $L_h$ induces an equivalence
        \[
        \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex}}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_h^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{h,Sch}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}),
        \]
        where the subscript $\otimes_? / \operatorname{lax}$ indicates two separate formulas, one for symmetric monoidal functors and the other for lax monoidal functors.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The proofs of \cite[Section 3]{KKandE} can be readily adapted to this situation. The Real structure poses no extra difficulty. Note that the key point for the left-exact assertions is that the category of separable $G$-$C^*$-algebras becomes a category of fibrant objects with fibrations as the Schochet fibrations and weak equivalences as the homotopy equivalences.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
\label{rem: S is loops}
    For later use, we explicitly mention an easy corollary of \Cref{prop: RALGseph omnibus}.4: we have an equivalence of functors
    \[
    L_h \circ (C_0(\mathbb R^{0,1},-)) \simeq \Omega \circ L_h : \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}.
    \]
    The details are exactly the same as in \cite[Example 3.19]{KKandE}.

    We also mention at this juncture that all the subsequent localizations leading to $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ will be left-exact Dwyer-Kan localizations. Hence we can take $C_0(\mathbb R^{0,1},-)$ (descended to the category under consideration) as a model for the loops functor in each of the subsequent localizations.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop: S to C to Cl fib seqn in homotopy cat}
    There exists a fiber sequence in $\mathsf G_2\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ of the form
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: s fib seqn}
        \mathcal{S} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_0} \mathbb{C} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{\iota}} Cl^{0,1},
    \end{equation}
    where $\iota$ is the canonical inclusion of $\mathbb{C} \cong Cl^{0,0}$ into $Cl^{0,1}$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
This is immediate from \Cref{eqn: mapping cone for s} and \Cref{example: mapping cone sequence is Schochet}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- defi-8: body_md -->
\hfill
\begin{itemize}
    \item A morphism $f: A \rightarrow B$ in $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is said to be a \emph{${\mathcal{K}_G}$-equivalence} if the induced map
        \[
        f \otimes 1_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}: A \otimes {\mathcal{K}_G} \rightarrow B \otimes {\mathcal{K}_G}
        \]
        is a homotopy equivalence.
    \item For any $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$, a functor $F: \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}$ is said to be \emph{$G$-stable} if for every isometric embedding of separable $G$-Hilbert spaces $V'\hookrightarrow V$, with $V' \neq 0$, and for all objects $A \in \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$, the induced map $F(A \otimes \mathcal{K}(V)) \rightarrow F(A \otimes \mathcal{K}(V'))$ is an equivalence.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defi-8 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
It is easy to see that a homotopy invariant functor on $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ inverts ${\mathcal{K}_G}$-equivalences if and only if is $G$-stable. See \cite[Proposition 2.2]{NAD} for a proof. It so turns out that inverting the $\mathcal{K}_G$-equivalences enables one to control the mapping spaces in the localization, whereas to verify that a homotopy invariant functor indeed inverts $\mathcal{K}_G$-equivalences, one usually just checks $G$-stability.
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- defi-9: body_md -->
Denote by $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ the Dwyer-Kan localization of $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ at $L_h(\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{K}_G})$, and denote by
    \[
    L_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}: \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}
    \] the localization functor.
<!-- end defi-9 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop: SKGRALKGseph omnibus}
    \hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $\infty$-category $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is canonically equivalent to the full-subcategory of $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ spanned by ${\mathcal{K}_G}$-stable algebras. When $G$ is compact, the functor $L_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}$ is in fact the left-adjoint of a left Bousfield localization.
        \item $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ has finite limits and countable coproducts. $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}$ preserves finite products and countable coproducts. $L_{\mathcal{K}_G}$ is left-exact.
        \item For every left-exact $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$, the equivalence in \Cref{eqn: SKGRALGseph uni prop} restricts to an equivalence
        \begin{equation}\label{eqn: lex skg uni prop}
            \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex}}(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},Sch}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}).
        \end{equation}
        \item Countable coproducts in $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ are given by countable direct sums of the respective $C^*$-algebras. The canonical map from a binary (resp. countable) coproduct to a binary (resp. countable) product in $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is an equivalence, whence $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is a semi-additive $\infty$-category.
        \item For every left-exact semi-additive $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$ with countable coproducts, the equivalence in \Cref{eqn: lex skg uni prop} restricts to an equivalence
        \begin{equation}\label{eqn: skg uni prop for sym mon}
              \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex},\coprod_{\omega}}(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},Sch,\oplus_\omega}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}),
        \end{equation}
        where the superscripts $\coprod_\omega, \oplus_\omega$ denote countable coproduct and countable sum preserving functors, respectively.
        \item $L_{\mathcal{K}_G}: \mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ has a symmetric monoidal refinement for both the tensor products on $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Consequently the same assertion is also true for $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}$. Moreover, the functors \[\otimes_?:\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \times \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}\rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}\] are bi-left exact and bi-countable coproduct preserving for $? \in \{\operatorname{min,max}\}$.
        \item For every symmetric monoidal left-exact semi-additive $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$ with countable coproducts, the pullback along the symmetric monoidal refinement of $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}$ induces an equivalence
        \[
        \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex},\coprod_\omega}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},Sch,\oplus_\omega}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}).
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
This follows by combining the approaches in \cite[Section 4]{KKandE}, \cite[Remark 3.34]{EisCASS} and \cite[Lemma 3.18, Corollary 3.19]{DJ}. The Real structure poses no extra difficulty.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- defi-10: body_md -->
Denote by $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ the Dwyer-Kan localization of $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ at $W_!$, and denote by
    \[
    L_{!,\oplus_\omega}: \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}}
    \] the localization functor.
<!-- end defi-10 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
It is a non-trivial property of classical $KK$- and $E$-categories for separable $C^*$-algebras that they have countable coproducts, which are furthermore modeled by countable direct sums of the respective $C^*$-algebras. If we do not close up $\hat{W}_!$ under countable sums, then there is no formal reason why our to-be-constructed $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ category will have countable coproducts (see the next paragraph too). The issue therefore arises when we want to extend $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ to the large category $\mathrm{KK}^{G}_{!,\infty}$ on all of $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}$: on the one hand, we can simply consider $\operatorname{Ind}_{\aleph_0}$-completion of $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$, but then we would destroy the countable coproducts which already exist in $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ (since \emph{a posteori} the homotopy category of $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ is equivalent to the classical bivariant $K$-categories), and would therefore be an unnatural object to consider. On the other hand, our current approach (as done in Section 3.7) of taking $\operatorname{Ind}_{\aleph_1}(\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}})$ would \emph{a priori} have no reason to have countable coproducts, but would have all uncountable filtered colimits, and would be yet another unnatural object! Of course, if we already know the comparison between the homotopy category of $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ and the classical bivariant $K$-categories, then the $\operatorname{Ind}_{\aleph_1}$-completion of $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ works out fine and becomes a presentable stable $\infty$-category, but we want to postpone this comparison until the very end. Thus, it calls for \emph{enforcing} that our $\mathrm{KK}_{!,\infty}^{G,\mathrm{sep}}$ categories have countable coproducts.   

    Having said that, we mention that the step of closing up $\hat{W}_!$ under countable sums is only relevant for non-separable algebras (and even then, more for the {aesthetic} features of our large categories). In particular, if the reader is only interested in separable $C^*$-algebras, then this step can be omitted, and one would still get a stable $\infty$-categorical refinement of the classical bivariant $K$-categories for separable $C^*$-algebras which would a fortiori have countable coproducts.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: SKGexcl omnibus}
    \hfill
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $\infty$-category $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is left-exact, semi-additive and posseses countable coproducts.
        \item The localization functor $L_{!,\oplus_\omega}$ is left-exact and countable sum preserving. The functor $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},!}$ is $!$-exact.
        \item For every left-exact semi-additive $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$ admitting countable coproducts, we have equivalences
        \begin{equation}
\label{uni prop excision iwthout symm mon}
\resizebox{0.95\textwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
\mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex},\coprod_\omega}
(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})
\xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{!,\oplus}^*}
\mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex},\coprod_\omega,\hat{W}_!}
(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})
\xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G}}^*}
\mathbf{Fun}^{{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},!+Sch,\oplus}_\omega}
(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}),
$}
\end{equation}
where the superscript $\hat{W}_!$  in the middle entity stands for functors on $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ which map morphisms in $\hat{W}_!$ to equivalences, and the superscript $!$ in the last entity stands for functors on $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ which map $!$-exact sequences to fiber sequences.
        \item When $!=\operatorname{se}$, \[L_{\operatorname{se},\oplus_\omega}: \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,\mathrm{se},\oplus_\omega}^{\mathrm{sep}}\] has a symmetric monoidal refinement for both the tensor products on $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$. When $!=\operatorname{ex}$, \[L_{\operatorname{ex},\oplus_\omega}: \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}} \rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,\mathrm{ex},\oplus_\omega}^{\mathrm{sep}}\] has a symmetric monoidal refinement for \emph{only} the maximal tensor product on $\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h}^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Consequently, the same assertions are true for $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},\operatorname{se},\oplus_\omega}$ and $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},\operatorname{ex},\oplus_\omega}$. 
        
        Moreover, the functors \[\otimes_?:\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}} \times \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}}\rightarrow \mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}}\] are bi-left exact and bi-countable coproduct preserving (for every choice of $(?,!)$ except $(\operatorname{min,ex})$).
        \item For every symmetric monoidal left-exact semi-additive $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}$ admitting countable coproducts, the pullback along the symmetric monoidal refinement of $L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},!,\oplus_\omega}$ (as discussed in the previous assertion) induces an equivalence
        \begin{equation}\label{eqn: uni prop excision}
            \mathbf{Fun}^{\operatorname{lex},\coprod_\omega}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathrm S_{{\mathcal{K}_G}}\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}_{h,!,\oplus}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D})  \xrightarrow[\simeq]{L_{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},!,\oplus_\omega}^*} \mathbf{Fun}^{{h,{\mathcal{K}_G},!+Sch,\oplus_{\omega}}}_{\otimes_?/\operatorname{lax}}(\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}},\mathcal{D}). 
        \end{equation}   
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
This follows by combining the approaches in \cite[Section 5]{KKandE} and \cite[Remark 3.35]{EisCASS}. Note that closing up $\hat{W}_!$ under countable sums has only been considered in \cite{EisCASS}, and an argument for the localization $L_{!,\oplus_\omega}$ to be countable coproduct preserving is omitted in loc.\! cit.\! This however follows from a dual version of \cite[Theorem 2.6.4]{RSW}\footnote{note that loc.\! cit.\! is written with cofibration categories, whereas our current business is with fibration categories. However, loc.\! cit.\! uses \cite[Proposition 7.7.1]{CIS} in the proof, which is indeed written with fibration categories.}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{prop: automatic Schochet exactness}
    Any homotopy invaraint and $!$-exact functor from $\mathsf G\mathsf C^{*}\!\mathsf{Alg}^{\mathrm{sep}}$ to a stable $\infty$-category is automatically Schochet exact.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The proof can be taken directly from \cite[Lemma 5.2]{KKandE}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- notn-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb R^{p,q}$ denote the Real space $\mathbb R^{p+q}$, with the involution $\kappa_{p,q}$ given by \[\kappa_{p,q}(x_1,x_2,...,x_{p+q})=(-x_1,-x_2,...,-x_p,x_{p+1},x_{p+2},...,x_{p+q}).\]  Denote by $\mathbb{S}^{p,q}$ the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{p,q}$ with the induced involution.
<!-- end notn-4 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: real toep extn}
    There exists a semi-split extension of Real $C^*$-algebras
    \[
    0\rightarrow \mathcal{K}(l^2\mathbb N) \rightarrow \mathcal{T}^{R} \rightarrow C(\mathbb{S}^{1,1}),
    \]
    where $\mathcal{T}^R$ is the Real isometry classfier $C^*$-algebra, i.e., there is a distinguised Real isometry $v$ in $\mathcal{T}^{R}$ such that for any unital (non-equivariant) Real $C^*$-algebra $A$, there is a bijection of sets 
    \[
    {\operatorname{Hom}}_u(\mathcal{T}^R,A) \xrightarrow{\cong} \operatorname{Isom}(A),~~~~~ \varphi \mapsto \varphi(v)
    \]
    between the set of unital, Real homomorphisms from $\mathcal{T}^R$ to $A$ and the set of Real isometries in $A$.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem: TR universal}
    The Real $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{T}^R$ as defined in \Cref{prop: real toep extn} exists.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Recall that the complex Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal{T^\mathbb C}$, given by the $C^*$-subalgebra generated by the unilateral shift (denoted $\boldsymbol{\iota}$ from now on) in $\mathcal{B}(l^2(\mathbb N))$, is the universal (complex) isometry classifier (\cite{COB}). It therefore follows that one model for $\mathcal{T}^R$ is $\mathcal{T}^{\mathbb C}$ equipped with the unique Real structure such that the unilateral shift is fixed by it. It is also easily seen to be the same as the Real $C^*$-subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(l^2(\mathbb N))$ generated by the unilateral shift, where the Real structure on the Hilbert space $l^2(\mathbb N)$ is by complex conjugation (as always).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
$C(\mathbb{S}^{1,1})$ is the Real unitary classifier $C^*$-algebra.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Again as before, the complex version of this result is well-known, see for example \cite[Proposition 2.3.4]{SOBERS}. It follows that the Real structure on the $C^*$-algebra of continuous functions on the circle should be so defined that the identity function on the circle is a Real unitary. Since the Real structure on the codomain $\mathbb C$ is complex conjugation, it directly follows from the definitions that the Real structure stemming from the Real space $\mathbb{S}^{1,1}$ is indeed the right one.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The morphism $\mathcal{T}^R \xrightarrow{} C(\mathbb{S}^{1,1})$ is given by mapping $\boldsymbol{\iota}$ (in the concrete model of $\mathcal{T}^R$ mentioned in \Cref{lem: TR universal}) to the inclusion $\mathbb{S}^{1,1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb C$. The kernel of $\varphi$ contains \[\boldsymbol{\iota}^n(1_{l^2\mathbb N}-\boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\iota}^*){\boldsymbol{\iota}^*}^m~\forall~ n,m \geq 0,\] and therefore also contains the Real $C^*$-subalgebra $\mathcal{K}(l^2\mathbb N)$ of $\mathcal{B}(l^2(\mathbb N))$. It is well-known that upon forgetting the Real structure, the kernel of $\varphi$ is precisely $\mathcal{K}(l^2\mathbb N)$, see for example \cite[Section 2.4]{SOBERS}. This shows the existence of the extension.

    To show that it also admits a Real cpc-split, one directly checks that the cpc-split described in \cite[Remark 6.7]{KKandE} is a Real map.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor: real red toep extn}
    There exists a semi-split extension of Real $C^*$-algebras
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn: red toep eqn}
